chapter.name: India's Urban Landscape
chapter.blurb: What makes an area urban or rural and India's long urban legacy, population density and how to read it from a satellite view, the scale and process of urbanisation in India and the world, how locational advantage built cities such as Jamshedpur, Mumbai and Kolkata, specialised city economies from Bengaluru's IT hub to craft towns and pilgrimage cities, Delhi's growth into the National Capital Region and Gurugram's IT/BPO boom, cities as cultural hubs, the challenges cities face including air quality, slums and Bengaluru's lake crisis, and planning cities from Jaipur's 'Pink City' and Singapore to India's modern urban redevelopment projects.

scope_in.item: Define what makes an area urban: a concentration of human populations, different kinds of businesses and occupations, government institutions, often elaborate transport and communication systems, and elected local bodies responsible for infrastructure and amenities

Define what makes an area rural: villages with usually lower populations, close-knit communities, more agriculture-based occupations, fewer businesses, less elaborate transport and communication systems, governed by gram panchayats
State that the exact population figure at which a place becomes urban differs by country, with the chapter's own figures for Denmark (220), Japan (50,000) and India (5,000)
Name India's urban legacy: Harappan cities such as Dholavira, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi, and historical cities such as Vijayanagara, Varanasi and Ujjain, most still flourishing today
Describe Dholavira's features as captioned in Fig. 7.2: spread over 48 ha, with residential areas, fortifications, streets, complex water structures and large community grounds
Define population density, the role of a demographer, and the formula: population density = total population of a region divided by the area of the region in square kilometres

Read Fig. 7.3's satellite images of Village Asadpur Khera (Jhajjhar, Haryana) and Gurugram city to compare open, sparsely built land against dense, built-up land as a way of judging relative population density

State the United Nations estimate that 68 per cent of the world's population will live in cities by 2050, compared to 55 per cent now, and that India's urban population has grown from 17 per cent in 1951 to around 40 per cent in 2025
Read Fig. 7.4, the bar chart of the world's most populous cities in 2025, including that Kolkata and New Delhi are the two Indian cities shown and their approximate populations in crores
Define urbanisation as the population shift from rural to urban areas and the corresponding decrease in the proportion of people living in rural areas

Describe the stages of urbanisation in Fig. 7.6: rural origins with farm-related work; early urbanisation with a shift to secondary/tertiary sectors and emergence as small towns and trading centres; population growth as people are attracted in; development of new infrastructure and diversity of jobs; and expansion into metropolitan areas

Describe the Sakchi/Jamshedpur case study: chosen for proximity to rich iron ore deposits, the Tata family's planned township, Sir Dorabji Tata's hospital built before steel production began, the 1919 renaming, and its status today as the largest industrial city in Jharkhand

State the general rule that cities often develop based on a favourable geographical location -- near coastlines, rivers or trade routes -- and apply it to Mumbai's location on the Arabian Sea and Kolkata's nearness to the eastern coast as vital port cities for trade

Describe how the Bombay Stock Exchange of 1875 made Mumbai the financial capital of the nation, drawing talent and exposure to new ideas, and how its film industry started in the 1910s and was flourishing by the 1930s
Identify Mumbai infrastructure and landmarks named in the chapter's figures: the Taj Hotel and Gateway of India, the Bandra Worli Sea Link, the Coastal Road, and the Bandra Kurla Complex

Describe Bengaluru as the 'Silicon Valley of India', an IT hub built on a concentration of software firms, start-ups and higher education institutions, with the close link between industry and education driving innovation including AI-based products
State that Hyderabad has grown into a major centre for technology-based enterprises

Name the craft/industry specialisations of smaller urban centres: Moradabad for brass work, Ludhiana and Tirupur for textile production, Jaipur for handicrafts and gem jewellery, Channapatna for wooden toys, and Kanchipuram for silk sarees

Name Kochi, Indore, Lucknow and Nagpur as growing cities that are lucrative for companies because their cost of operations is lower than in larger cities, letting them serve customers across India and globally

Describe Agra's tourism economy around the Taj Mahal, attracting 70-80 lakh visitors a year, and Amritsar's and Varanasi's pilgrim-driven economies supporting transportation, hospitality, local food vending and handicrafts

Describe Delhi's history as a centre of culture, trade and administration from the Iron Age, with forts, roads and markets built by the Rajputs, Turks and Mughals, and the British building a new capital and introducing railways and electricity

Describe Delhi's post-Independence growth as capital of the Indian Republic, with ministries, industries, universities and research centres attracting people, and the resulting pressure on housing, water and sewerage systems

Describe the creation of the National Capital Region including NOIDA (New Okhla Industrial Development Authority) and Ghaziabad, and how better roads, highways and the metro rail system boosted the region's expansion

Describe Gurugram's growth since the 1990s into a major IT and BPO hub, and define Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) as a company hiring another service provider to do specific business functions or processes, reducing costs and gaining expert professionals
Identify Fig. 7.16's Rashtrapati Bhawan and Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi
Explain how cities draw people from various regions and create a potpourri of shared culture, languages, customs, traditions, food and festivals
Describe the vada pav example: a Maharashtrian-style potato dumpling placed inside a pav (whose bread and potatoes are themselves Portuguese), which became popular among Mumbai's textile mill workers

Describe Kolkata's institutions surviving from its time as capital of British-ruled India (the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial) and its annual Durga Puja, a five-day autumn festival inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2021

Describe how cities allocate resources to cultural centres, libraries, museums and sports stadiums as hubs for socio-cultural enrichment, and create spaces for gatherings that help residents interact, build relationships and form networks

Identify Fig. 7.17's examples of cultural hubs: the Indian Museum, street art in Delhi, stadiums, an open-air music festival, Durga Puja celebrations, commuter interaction, and the Pradhanmantri Sangrahalay in New Delhi

Describe the pressures an influx of large populations puts on a city's resources and infrastructure: demand for food, water, energy and housing; narrow and poorly maintained roads; unplanned residential areas with poor access to services; growing vehicle numbers; and rising temperatures from 'heat islands'
Define the Air Quality Index (AQI) per the chapter's glossary, and state that the National Capital Region frequently records AQI levels over 400, far above the safe limit of 50
State that urban areas often have higher crime rates than rural regions due to higher population density and economic inequality, requiring greater policing and law enforcement

Define slums as overcrowded city settlements with poor housing and limited water, sanitation and municipal services, generally growing near a city's periphery, railway tracks or industrial areas due to a lack of affordable housing
Identify Fig. 7.18's collage of urban challenges: poor air quality, water scarcity, traffic jams, reduced green spaces, waste generation, flooding during monsoons, and urban slums

Describe the informal work slum dwellers perform to support cities -- vegetable vending, domestic help, laundry services, construction work, plumbing -- and the Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana's aim of providing affordable housing to economically weaker households

Describe Bengaluru's lake crisis: causes including overuse of groundwater, lack of rainwater harvesting and encroachment of lake beds; the fall from around 1,000 lakes to about 200; the Bellandur and Varthur lakes getting covered in foam, releasing toxic gases and catching fire; and community-led revival through non-profits, Resident Welfare Associations and communities using desilting, repairing bunds with natural materials, clearing drainage channels, planting native species and restocking fish

State the factors an urban planner must address: population, the kinds of jobs people have, transportation needs, the location of homes, businesses, parks and public facilities, and public safety provisions

Describe Jaipur's planning as the 'Pink City': Vidyadhar Bhattacharya as chief architect and urban planner appointed by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in 1727, the grid pattern of rectangular blocks (chowkris) aligned to the cardinal directions, wide streets, open spaces, gardens and nine public squares, the 20-foot wall with seven gates, and the pink sandstone giving a uniform, cohesive look

Describe how Jaipur's design allowed good sunlight, fresh air and a steady water supply through reservoirs and canals suited to the local dry climate, and that markets were built with shaded porches for traders and travellers

Describe Singapore's population density (over 8,000 people per sq km), its Concept Plan looking up to 40 years ahead and Master Plan updated every 5 years, and its transformation from an overcrowded port in the 1960s to a modern city-state

Describe Singapore's mixed-use spaces (such as Marina Bay Sands and Raffles Place), its mass public transport system (rail, buses, cycling paths, green walking corridors), and its sustainable high-rise buildings with rooftop and vertical gardens that earned it the title of a 'garden city'

Describe Singapore's walkability, its integration of senior housing with healthcare, childcare and green spaces, and its status as one of the world's 'blue zone' cities, with Okinawa in Japan as the chapter's example of another blue zone

Describe India's urban redevelopment examples: Ahmedabad's Sabarmati Riverfront with its promenades, parks, markets and the pedestrian-and-cycle Atal Bridge, and Gangtok's pedestrian-only Mahatma Gandhi Road

Describe the chapter's concluding reflection: cities as living organisms that are both centres of consumption and production, and the ICT tools named as needed for convenient and sustainable urban life -- intelligent traffic systems, digital surveillance, online grievance redressal platforms and solar-powered public spaces

concepts.name: Urban and rural areas, and India's urban legacy
concepts.description: What makes an area urban and what makes it rural, the bodies that govern each, how the population figure at which a place becomes urban differs from country to country, and the cities India has had since Harappan times.
concepts.idea: There is no single worldwide rule for when a settlement becomes a city; what a city actually is shows up in what it concentrates -- people, businesses, institutions and transport -- rather than in any one number.
concepts.rule: Cities, also called urban areas, have a concentration of human populations, different kinds of businesses and occupations, government institutions, and often elaborate transportation and communication systems, and they have elected local bodies responsible for the development of infrastructure and other amenities. Rural areas consist of villages that usually have lower populations, close-knit communities, a larger number of agriculture-based occupations, fewer businesses and generally less elaborate transport and communication systems, and they are governed by gram panchayats. The exact definitions of urban and rural differ across the world: a place becomes urban if its population exceeds 220 in Denmark, 50,000 in Japan and 5,000 in India.
concepts.example: India's urban legacy runs from Harappan cities such as Dholavira, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi to historical ones such as Vijayanagara, Varanasi and Ujjain, most of which are still flourishing today. Dholavira alone was spread over 48 ha with residential areas, fortifications, streets, complex water structures and large community grounds.

questions.q: The chapter shows cities in two very different pictures -- a Harappan site such as Dholavira, and a modern area of concentrated population and business. Analyse what the two pictures have in common.
questions.a: Sample: Dholavira had residential areas, fortifications, streets, complex water structures and large community grounds over 48 ha; a city today has a concentration of people, many kinds of businesses and occupations, government institutions and elaborate transport. The materials and the technology are utterly different, but both are places where a large number of people live close together and share built facilities that no single household could provide for itself -- water works and community grounds then, transport and communication systems now. What the two pictures share is the idea of shared infrastructure serving a concentrated population, which is why the chapter treats both as urban.
s: Sets out what each picture contains
Identifies the common element -- a concentrated population sharing built facilities
Notes that the difference lies in the technology and scale rather than in the idea

questions.q: Denmark calls a place urban above 220 people while Japan does so only above 50,000. Analyse what this gap suggests, and what it means for comparing one country's urban share with another's.
questions.a: Sample: The two figures are more than two hundred times apart, yet both are called the line between rural and urban. A figure that low in Denmark suggests that its ordinary settlements are small, so 220 already marks a place out as a centre; a figure that high in Japan suggests that settlements of several thousand are so common there that they are not treated as anything special. Each country has therefore fitted the word 'urban' to its own settlement pattern rather than to a shared standard. The consequence is that the urban share of two countries cannot simply be placed side by side: a Danish village of 300 counts in Denmark's urban figure while a Japanese town of 30,000 does not count in Japan's. Any such comparison has to carry each country's own definition with it.
s: States the two thresholds and how far apart they are
Offers a reason why a country might set the line where it does
Explains that each country fits the word to its own pattern rather than a common standard
Concludes that urban shares are not directly comparable without the definitions

questions.q: The chapter describes rural areas largely by what they have less of than cities -- fewer businesses, lower populations, less elaborate transport. Evaluate whether that is a fair way to describe a village.
questions.a: Sample: It is accurate as far as it goes, and it makes the contrast easy to see, which is what the introduction needs. But it measures the village against the city and reports only the shortfall. The chapter itself supplies what that leaves out when it mentions close-knit communities -- a positive feature, not a lack -- and a larger number of agriculture-based occupations, which is what feeds the city as well. A description built out of absences also hides the fact that the village has its own elected body, the gram panchayat. So the description is fair as a comparison but incomplete as a portrait, and the chapter's own words about close-knit communities show it knows this.
s: States what the comparison does well -- it makes the contrast clear
Identifies the limitation -- describing a village by its shortfalls against a city
Reaches a judgement supported by the chapter's own positive details, such as close-knit communities or the gram panchayat

Asks about the governing body, transport or institutions and names which answer points to urban

concepts.name: Population density, and reading it from a satellite view
concepts.description: What population density means, the formula demographers use and the unit it is expressed in, and how a top-down satellite view lets you compare how densely or sparsely a village and a city are settled.
concepts.idea: Crowding is not the same thing as size: a place feels crowded because of how many people share each unit of area, which is why density, and not the total population, is what tells you how a place lives.
concepts.rule: The distribution of the number of people within a specific area reflects how densely or sparsely crowded a place is. Experts known as demographers assess the number of people living per unit of area, which is called population density, and it is usually expressed as the number of people per square kilometre. Population density = total population of a region divided by the area of the region in square kilometres.
concepts.example: In Fig. 7.3 the satellite view of Village Asadpur Khera in Jhajjhar, Haryana shows large blocks of green and brown land, which are open areas, while the view of Gurugram city in the same state shows a grey built-up area with a complex network of buildings -- the city is far more densely settled than the village.

questions.q: Explain how a satellite view helps in judging how densely a place is settled, and what it cannot tell you on its own.
questions.a: A satellite view is a top-down view of the earth's surface, so it shows at a glance how much of an area is built up and how much is open. Large blocks of green and brown land suggest open ground and sparse settlement, while a grey network of buildings suggests a densely built area. What it cannot give on its own is a number: the actual population density needs the total population and the area of the region, which the picture does not supply.
s: Explains that the view shows the proportion of built-up land to open land
Links the built-up grey network to dense settlement and the open green and brown blocks to sparse settlement
Notes that the picture alone gives no figure, since density needs the population and the area

questions.q: A region has a population of 60,000 spread over an area of 4 square kilometres. What is its population density?
questions.a: 15,000 people per square kilometre
o: 15,000 people per square kilometre
2,40,000 people per square kilometre
240 people per square kilometre
4 people per square kilometre

questions.q: A village has 1,200 people living over 3 square kilometres. Work out its population density, showing what you divided by what.
questions.a: Population density = total population divided by the area in square kilometres = 1,200 divided by 3 = 400. So the village has a population density of 400 people per square kilometre.
s: Sets up the division as population divided by area, that is 1,200 divided by 3
Gives the answer as 400 people per square kilometre

questions.q: Town P has 90,000 people in 9 square kilometres. Town Q has 60,000 people in 5 square kilometres. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Q is more densely populated than P, although P has more people
o: Q is more densely populated than P, although P has more people
P is more densely populated than Q, because P has more people
Both have the same population density
Density cannot be compared unless the two towns are in the same state

questions.q: A city covers 50 square kilometres and has a population density of 12,000 people per square kilometre. Find its total population, and say how you worked it out.
questions.a: Density is the population divided by the area, so the population is the density multiplied by the area. That gives 12,000 multiplied by 50, which is 6,00,000 people.
s: States that the population is the density multiplied by the area, reversing the formula
Gives the answer as 6,00,000 people

questions.q: Over ten years a town's population doubles while its area stays the same, and a neighbouring town's area doubles while its population stays the same. Using the chapter's formula, say what happens to each town's population density and why.
questions.a: In the first town the population on the top of the division doubles while the area below it is unchanged, so the density doubles -- twice as many people now share each square kilometre. In the second town the population on the top is unchanged while the area below it doubles, so the density falls to half -- the same people are spread over twice as much ground. The two cases show that density depends on both parts of the division, not on population alone.
s: States that the first town's density doubles, because the population rises while the area is unchanged
States that the second town's density falls to half, because the area rises while the population is unchanged
Draws the point that density depends on both the population and the area

questions.q: A district officer has the population of every village and town in her district but not their areas. Using this chapter, explain what she can and cannot say about crowding, and what she would need in order to complete the picture.
questions.a: Sample: With populations alone she can say which settlements are the largest, and she can rank them by total number of people. She cannot say which is the most crowded, because the chapter defines population density as the total population divided by the area in square kilometres, and she is missing the second of those two figures. A small town of 20,000 packed into two square kilometres is far more densely settled than a sprawling one of 40,000 over twenty. To complete the picture she would need the area of each settlement in square kilometres; a satellite view would also help her see how much of that area is built up and how much is open.
s: States what population figures alone allow -- a comparison of size
States what they do not allow, and why: density needs the area as well
Names what is needed -- the area in square kilometres, and optionally the satellite view as support

questions.q: Assertion (A): The most populous region of a country need not be its most crowded. Reason (R): Population density is the total population divided by the area of the region, so a large population spread over a large area can give a low density. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The chapter introduces population density through a get-together at home rather than through the formula. Analyse what that choice achieves and what it leaves for the formula to do.
questions.a: Sample: The get-together gives the reader the feeling first. Everyone has experienced a room that is comfortable with four people and unbearable with thirty, so the idea that crowding depends on people per unit of space arrives before any arithmetic and needs no explaining. What the example cannot do is compare. It gives no way of saying whether Gurugram is twice or twenty times as crowded as Asadpur Khera, and it gives no unit. The formula supplies exactly that -- a single number in people per square kilometre that can be set beside any other place's number. So the example carries the meaning and the formula carries the measurement.
s: Explains what the everyday example achieves -- it conveys the idea through familiar experience
Identifies its limit -- it cannot compare places or give a number
States what the formula adds: a comparable figure in people per square kilometre

questions.q: Two neighbourhoods in the same city are found to have the same population density. Analyse why their residents might still experience very different levels of crowding, using the chapter's own picture of a dense settlement.
questions.a: Sample: Density is a single average over a whole area, and an average hides how the people are arranged inside it. In one neighbourhood the same number of people per square kilometre could be living in high-rise buildings with open ground, parks and wide roads between them; in the other they could be packed into low buildings covering almost every metre, with the grey, complex network of construction that the chapter's satellite view of a city shows. The number is the same but the experience is not, because one has shared open space and the other has none. The chapter's own satellite images make this visible: they distinguish open green and brown blocks from built-up grey, which is something the density figure alone cannot report. So density is a useful summary but it needs the picture beside it.
s: States that density is an average over an area
Describes two arrangements that give the same figure -- for example high-rise with open space against fully built-up low construction
Connects this to the chapter's satellite view, which distinguishes open land from built-up land
Concludes that the figure needs to be read together with how the area is actually built

questions.q: The chapter asks you to infer the population density of a village and a city from satellite images alone. Evaluate whether that is a sound way to reach such a conclusion.
questions.a: Sample: It is sound for a comparison and unsound for a measurement. The images genuinely carry evidence: open green and brown blocks against a dense grey network of buildings is a real difference, and concluding that Gurugram is more densely settled than Asadpur Khera from them is safe. What the images cannot support is any figure, because the chapter's own formula needs the total population and the area, and neither is visible from above. There is also a risk in the inference, since buildings are not people -- an area of empty new construction would look dense and be nearly unpeopled. So the method is good for ranking two places and should not be pushed further than that.
s: Accepts that the images support a comparison between the two places
Identifies the limit -- no figure can be read off, since population and area are not visible
Adds a caution and reaches an overall judgement, for example that buildings are not the same as people

questions.q: Design a short classroom activity that would let your class work out and compare the population density of two areas near your school. Set out the steps and the unit you would report.
questions.a: Sample: First, choose two areas of different character, say a residential colony and a stretch of farmland at the edge of town. Second, find the area of each in square kilometres, using a map or a satellite view to trace its boundary. Third, get the number of people living in each, from local records or by counting households and multiplying by the average household size. Fourth, divide the population by the area for each, and report both results in people per square kilometre so that they can be set side by side. Finally, put the two satellite views next to the two figures and check that the more crowded-looking image is the one with the higher number.
s: Describes getting the area of each place in square kilometres
Describes getting the population of each place
States the division and reports the result in people per square kilometre for both, allowing a comparison

concepts.name: The scale of urbanisation and the stages of the urbanisation process
concepts.description: What urbanisation means, how large the shift to cities has become in the world and in India, what the chart of the world's most populous cities shows, and the stages through which a farming area becomes a metropolitan one.
concepts.idea: Urbanisation is not a single event but a sequence -- work changes first, then people arrive, then infrastructure follows, and only then does the place become a metropolitan area.
concepts.rule: Urbanisation is the population shift from rural to urban areas and the corresponding decrease in the proportion of people living in rural areas. Fig. 7.6 sets out the process in stages: rural origins with farm-related work; early urbanisation, a shift to secondary and tertiary sectors such as small-scale industries, transport and services, and emergence as small towns and trading centres; this attracts people from other areas and the population grows; new infrastructure develops -- factories, hotels, government institutions, banks, entertainment and sports -- along with a diversity of jobs; and finally cities expand to form metropolitan areas with large populations, high-rise buildings, shopping malls, a metro and a busy transport network.
concepts.example: According to United Nations estimates, 68 per cent of the world's population will be living in cities by 2050, compared to 55 per cent now, and India's urban population has grown from 17 per cent in 1951 to around 40 per cent in 2025.

questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Explain, using Fig. 7.6, why urbanisation is described as a gradual transition rather than a sudden change.
questions.a: Fig. 7.6 shows the change happening in stages rather than at once. It begins with rural origins and farm-related work; then work shifts to secondary and tertiary sectors such as small-scale industries, transport and services, and the place emerges as a small town or trading centre; this attracts people from other areas and the population grows; new infrastructure and a diversity of jobs follow; and only at the end do cities expand to form metropolitan areas. Each step depends on the one before it, which is why the chapter calls it a gradual transition from villages to small towns to bustling megacities.
s: Names the starting point, rural origins with farm-related work
Describes at least two middle stages in order, such as the shift of sectors and the growth of population and infrastructure
States the end point, expansion into metropolitan areas, and notes that each stage follows from the one before

questions.q: A farming village sets up a few small workshops and a bus service, and a weekly market begins to draw traders from nearby villages. Which stage of Fig. 7.6 does this match?

o: Early urbanisation -- a shift to secondary and tertiary sectors, with emergence as a small town and trading centre
Rural origins, where the work is farm-related
The development of new infrastructure such as hotels, banks and government institutions
Expansion of the city to form a metropolitan area

questions.q: A town that had mostly farmers twenty years ago now has an auto driver, a writer, a musician, an architect and a security guard living on one street. Which part of the urbanisation process does this illustrate, and what usually comes with it?
questions.a: It illustrates the diversity of jobs that Fig. 7.6 places after people have been attracted to the town and its population has grown. The same stage brings the development of new infrastructure -- factories, hotels, government institutions, banks, entertainment and sports facilities -- which is what creates those varied kinds of work.
s: Identifies it as the diversity of jobs stage of the urbanisation process
Links it to the development of new infrastructure that comes with that stage

questions.q: In 1951 about 17 out of every 100 Indians lived in urban areas; in 2025 the figure is around 40 out of every 100. Which statement about this change is supported by the chapter?

The number of people living in Indian villages must have fallen to zero in some states
India's urban share is now higher than the world's expected share for 2050

questions.q: Fig. 7.4 gives the population of the world's most populous cities in 2025 in crores, with Jakarta the highest at 4.19. Using the chapter's own caption, say what the chart is meant to show about India.
questions.a: The caption says that two of the most populated cities in the world are in India -- Kolkata and New Delhi. So the chart is meant to show that India is not simply urbanising in general but already has cities among the largest anywhere, which is why the chapter places it beside the figures for India's rising urban share.
s: States that the chart places two Indian cities, Kolkata and New Delhi, among the world's most populous

questions.q: A district has a new highway, and a village along it has begun to change. Using Fig. 7.6, predict the order in which three further changes are likely to appear there.
questions.a: First the work would begin to shift away from farming towards small-scale industries, transport and services, and the village would start to serve as a small trading centre. Next, those opportunities would attract people from other areas and the population would grow. Then new infrastructure would follow -- shops, banks, a hotel, government offices -- bringing a wider variety of jobs, and in time the place could expand towards a larger urban area.
s: Puts the shift to secondary and tertiary work and the trading centre first
Puts the arrival of people and population growth next
Puts the new infrastructure and diversity of jobs after that, leading towards expansion

questions.q: The chapter says a similar trend to the world's is expected in India, but gives no figure for India in 2050. Using only what the chapter does state, explain what can and cannot be claimed about India's urban future.
questions.a: Sample: What can be claimed is the direction. The chapter states that India's urban share rose from 17 per cent in 1951 to around 40 per cent in 2025, and that a trend similar to the world's is expected, so it is fair to say the share is expected to keep rising. What cannot be claimed is any particular figure for India in 2050. The 68 per cent belongs to the United Nations estimate for the world, not for India, and the chapter deliberately says only 'a similar trend' rather than giving a number. Borrowing the world figure and calling it India's would be putting a number into the chapter that the chapter refuses to give.
s: States what is supported: the direction of change, from 17 per cent in 1951 to around 40 per cent in 2025 and expected to continue
States what is not supported: any specific figure for India in 2050
Explains that 68 per cent is the world estimate and must not be transferred to India

questions.q: Assertion (A): United Nations estimates say that by 2050 a majority of the world's population will still be living in rural areas. Reason (R): Urbanisation is defined as the population shift from rural to urban areas, together with the corresponding decrease in the proportion of people living in rural areas. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false

questions.q: In Fig. 7.6 the growth of population is placed after the shift of work to other sectors, not before it. Analyse why that order makes sense.
questions.a: Sample: People move for reasons, and in this chapter's account the reason is work. Fig. 7.6 has the place first shift to secondary and tertiary sectors -- small-scale industries, transport, services -- and emerge as a small town and trading centre. Only once those opportunities exist does the diagram say it attracts people from other areas and the population grows. Put the other way round, a crowd arriving in a purely farming village would find nothing to do, and the chapter's own examples follow the same order: the steel plant came to Sakchi and the people followed. So the order is not decorative -- it says that opportunity pulls population, rather than population creating opportunity.
s: States the order the diagram gives: the change of work comes before the growth of population
Explains why that order is sensible, namely that people move towards opportunities
Supports it with the chapter's own pattern or with what would follow if the order were reversed

questions.q: Fig. 7.4 shows city populations in 2025 while the text gives the world's urban share for 2050. Analyse what each of the two measures tells you that the other does not, and why the chapter needs both.
questions.a: Sample: The chart measures individual cities. It says that Jakarta at 4.19 crore is the largest of those shown and that Kolkata and New Delhi are among the world's most populous, so it tells you how big single places have become. What it cannot tell you is whether the world as a whole is becoming urban, since ten cities are not the world. The percentage does exactly the opposite: 55 per cent now rising to an expected 68 per cent by 2050 tells you that the balance between rural and urban living is shifting everywhere, but it names no city and gives no sense of the scale any one of them has reached. The chapter needs both because its subject is urbanisation in two senses at once -- more people living in cities, and cities themselves growing very large -- and a reader given only one of the two figures would miss half the change.
s: States what the chart of individual cities shows, with an accurate detail from it
States what the percentage shows about the rural-urban balance
Identifies what each measure cannot show on its own
Concludes why the chapter needs both together

questions.q: Fig. 7.6 ends with metropolitan areas, large populations, high-rise buildings, shopping malls and a busy transport network. Evaluate whether that is a satisfactory place for the diagram to stop.
questions.a: Sample: As a description of how a place becomes a city, stopping there is reasonable -- the diagram has taken the reader from farm work to a metropolitan area and shown each step in between. But the chapter itself does not stop there, and the diagram is the poorer for doing so. Within two pages the text is describing pressure on food, water, energy and housing, heat islands, air quality index levels over 400 against a safe limit of 50, and the growth of slums. A diagram that ends with malls and a metro reads as though the process were simply an improvement. Adding a final box for the strains that follow would have made it truer to the chapter it introduces.
s: Grants what the diagram does well -- it traces the whole path from farm work to a metropolitan area
Identifies what it leaves out, naming at least one challenge the chapter itself raises later
Reaches a judgement about whether that is a satisfactory stopping point

questions.q: Write a short diary entry by someone who has lived in the same place for fifty years, describing the stages of Fig. 7.6 as she actually saw them happen. Use only the changes the diagram names.
questions.a: Sample: 'When I was small everyone here worked the fields, and the only journey anyone made was to the weekly market. Then the little workshops opened, and a bus began to run, and traders started coming in from the villages around; people took to calling us a town. After that the newcomers arrived, whole families of them, and the lanes filled up. The bank came, then the hotel, then the government office, and suddenly the neighbours were an architect and a musician and a security guard rather than farmers. Now there is a metro line where the last field was, and they tell me we are part of a metropolitan area.'
s: Begins from rural origins with farm-related work and moves to the shift of sectors and the trading centre
Includes the arrival of people, the new infrastructure and the diversity of jobs
Ends with expansion into a metropolitan area, adding nothing the diagram does not name

concepts.name: Locational advantage: Jamshedpur, Mumbai and Kolkata
concepts.description: How a favourable geographical location -- nearness to raw materials, coastlines or trade routes -- turns a place into an economic hub, using the chapter's case studies of Sakchi/Jamshedpur, Mumbai and Kolkata.
concepts.idea: A location that made sense for one reason -- iron ore nearby, a coastline for ships -- can go on attracting a completely different kind of economic activity decades later, once the first advantage has drawn in people, money and infrastructure.
concepts.rule: Cities often develop based on a favourable geographical location. Places near coastlines, rivers, or important trade routes tend to become economic hubs, as do places near agricultural produce and raw materials that support artisan communities and manufacturing. They become centres of economic activity as well as political and administrative power.
concepts.example: Sakchi, a small village in the Chota Nagpur Plateau, was chosen as the site for Asia's first steel plant for its proximity to rich iron ore deposits; the Tata family built it into a planned township with wide tree-lined streets and civic amenities, and Sir Dorabji Tata built a hospital there before steel production even began. Renamed Jamshedpur in 1919, it is today the largest industrial city in Jharkhand. Mumbai's location along the Arabian Sea and Kolkata's nearness to the eastern coast made them vital port cities for domestic and international trade; with the setting up of the Bombay Stock Exchange in 1875, Mumbai also became the financial capital of the nation, and its film industry started in the 1910s and was flourishing by the 1930s.

o: Sakchi becoming Jamshedpur

questions.a: The locational feature would be a coastline, as with Mumbai's position along the Arabian Sea, which makes shipping and trade easier. questions.q: Two towns each sit beside a river. Town X has no raw materials or trade routes nearby; Town Y is close to rich mineral deposits and lies on an old trading route. Based on this chapter's rule about locational advantage, which is more likely to grow into an economic hub, and why?

o: Town Y, because nearness to raw materials and trade routes is what the chapter says tends to create economic hubs

questions.q: Using the chapter's Jamshedpur example, explain how a single planned decision -- building a hospital before the factory even started production -- fits into the town's wider development.
questions.a: The Tata family's vision was to develop the area into a township with modern facilities for all personnel working in the factory, and Sir Dorabji Tata's hospital was part of that same planned vision, built even before steel production began. It fits alongside the wide, tree-lined streets, gardens, open spaces, houses and other civic amenities that together turned Sakchi into a properly planned town rather than a mining camp.
s: Connects the hospital to the Tata family's wider vision of a township with modern facilities

questions.q: A historian says 'Jamshedpur is really two stories: one about geography, and one about planning.' Using this chapter, explain what each of the two stories is.
questions.a: The geography story is that Sakchi was chosen because of its proximity to rich iron ore deposits -- a locational advantage the town did nothing to create. The planning story is what the Tata family did with that advantage: a deliberate township with wide tree-lined streets, gardens, open spaces, houses, civic amenities and even a hospital built before steel production began, which is why more factories and people were attracted to the region afterwards.
s: Explains the geography story: the iron ore deposits that made the site attractive
Explains the planning story: the Tata family's deliberate township design
Links the planning to the further growth -- more factories and people drawn to the region

questions.q: The chapter says Mumbai's port location made it a hub for trade, and separately that the Bombay Stock Exchange made it the financial capital. Apply this distinction to explain why a coastline alone would not have been enough.
questions.a: Sample: A coastline on its own only gives ease of shipping -- it explains why goods could move in and out of Mumbai, which is what made it a port city for domestic and international trade. Becoming the financial capital needed something more: an institution, the Bombay Stock Exchange of 1875, that could gather capital, draw talent from all sections of society, and connect Mumbai to information and ideas from around the world. The chapter is careful to credit the two separately -- location for the port trade, the BSE for the financial-capital status -- which shows that geography opens a door but an institution is what a city walks through it with.
s: States what the coastline alone explains -- Mumbai's role as a port city for trade
States what the coastline alone does not explain -- financial-capital status
Names the Bombay Stock Exchange as the additional factor, with at least one of its effects such as congregating talent or spreading ideas

questions.q: Assertion (A): Mumbai became the financial capital of the nation. Reason (R): Mumbai's location is along the Arabian Sea, which made it a vital port city for domestic and international trade. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Analyse why the chapter tells the story of Jamshedpur through the hospital and the streets rather than through steel production figures.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter's point in this section is not how much steel Jamshedpur produced but how a locational advantage becomes a city. Steel output would only support the geography half of the story -- that iron ore was nearby. The hospital, the tree-lined streets and the civic amenities support the other half, that a location has to be deliberately built into a liveable town before it becomes a lasting city rather than a temporary mining camp. questions.q: Jamshedpur, Mumbai and Kolkata are all given in this concept as examples of locational advantage. Analyse whether the three owe their growth to the same kind of advantage or to different kinds.
questions.a: Sample: All three fit the chapter's general rule that a favourable geographical location can turn a place into an economic hub, but the advantage is not identical in each case. Jamshedpur's advantage was to raw material: proximity to rich iron ore deposits, which is a resource sitting in the ground and needing extraction and transport out. Mumbai's and Kolkata's advantage was to connection: a coastline, along the Arabian Sea and near the eastern coast respectively, that let goods and people move in and out by sea. A resource advantage like Jamshedpur's eventually runs into a limit, since the ore itself could in principle be exhausted, while a coastline is a standing advantage that does not deplete the way a mineral deposit can. Mumbai's case adds a further layer beyond even the coastline: the Bombay Stock Exchange of 1875 turned a trading advantage into a financial one, which is not a natural feature at all but an institution built on top of the location. So the three share the general principle of locational advantage but differ in whether the advantage is a resource, a connection, or an institution built using that connection.
s: Identifies Jamshedpur's advantage as a raw material -- iron ore deposits
Identifies Mumbai's and Kolkata's advantage as a coastline enabling trade connections
Notes a genuine difference between the two kinds of advantage, such as a resource being exhaustible while a coastline is a standing advantage

But the chapter's own account shows the coastline was only the start: it explains the port trade, not the financial-capital status, which the chapter attributes instead to the Bombay Stock Exchange, nor the film industry, which it attributes to the exchange of information and ideas that followed. So Mumbai supports the rule about coastlines only for the earliest layer of its growth; a reader who stopped at 'coastline' would miss why Mumbai looks the way it does today. The example is well chosen but needs the rest of the chapter's detail to be complete.

concepts.name: Specialised city economies: technology hubs, craft towns and tourism
concepts.description: How some cities specialise -- Bengaluru and Hyderabad in technology, smaller centres in a particular craft or industry, other cities in being lower-cost places to do business, and still others in tourism or pilgrimage.
concepts.idea: Not every city grows the same way: some become known for one thing in particular, and that one thing -- software, brass work, a monument, a pilgrimage -- is enough on its own to support an entire local economy.
concepts.rule: Bengaluru, the Silicon Valley of India, became an IT hub due to the concentration of software firms, start-ups and higher education institutions, with a close link between industry and education encouraging innovation; Hyderabad has similarly grown into a major centre for technology-based enterprises. Smaller, less populous urban centres specialise in certain industries -- for example Moradabad for brass work, Ludhiana and Tirupur for textile production, Jaipur for handicrafts and gem jewellery, Channapatna for wooden toys, and Kanchipuram for silk sarees. Other growing cities such as Kochi, Indore, Lucknow and Nagpur are lucrative for companies because their cost of operations is lower than in larger cities. Some cities draw economic activity from historical and cultural significance instead: Agra, with the Taj Mahal, attracts 70-80 lakh visitors every year, while Amritsar and Varanasi thrive on pilgrims, driving transportation, hospitality, local food vending and handicrafts.

questions.q: The chapter places Agra's tourism economy and Varanasi's pilgrimage economy in the same paragraph as the craft towns and the low-cost cities. Analyse whether tourism/pilgrimage economies really belong in the same category as the others, or whether they work differently.
questions.a: Sample: On the surface all four groups -- technology hubs, craft towns, low-cost cities and tourism/pilgrimage cities -- are alike in that each has one dominant driver of its economy. But the driver works differently in each case. A craft town or a technology hub sells something it makes -- toys, silk, software. A low-cost city sells the advantage of its own operating costs to outside companies. Agra and Varanasi, by contrast, sell almost nothing that leaves the city: their draw is the place itself, the Taj Mahal or the sacred sites, and the economic activity -- transportation, hospitality, food vending, handicrafts -- exists only because visitors physically travel there. That makes tourism and pilgrimage economies dependent on people continuing to come, in a way that a craft town's exports are not, so grouping them together captures a similarity of scale but blurs a real difference in how the money is actually earned.

On the other hand, resting an entire town's economy on one craft is a narrow base: the chapter's own account of Bengaluru shows that a hub built on a concentration of many linked firms and institutions can keep generating new products, such as AI-based ones, while a single craft has less obvious room to diversify. concepts.name: Delhi's growth from ancient capital to the National Capital Region
concepts.description: Delhi's long history as a centre of culture, trade and administration, its expansion after Independence, the pressures that growth created, and how the National Capital Region and Gurugram's IT/BPO boom answered those pressures.
concepts.idea: A city that has been a capital for thousands of years does not stop growing once it becomes a republic's capital -- the very success that keeps drawing people in is what forces the city to spill out beyond its own boundary.
concepts.rule: Delhi has thrived as a centre of culture, trade and administration from the Iron Age; the Rajputs, Turks and Mughals built forts, roads and markets, while the British built a new capital and introduced railways and electricity. After Independence, New Delhi became the capital of the Indian Republic, with many ministries, industries, universities and research centres attracting people for jobs and education from across the country. As the population expanded it put pressure on infrastructure like housing and water and sewerage systems. The creation of the National Capital Region, to include NOIDA (New Okhla Industrial Development Authority) and Ghaziabad, helped ease the pressure; better roads, highways and the metro rail system boosted the region's expansion. Since the 1990s Gurugram has become a major IT and BPO hub, drawing global companies and driving the development of housing and commercial spaces. A Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) is a company hiring another service provider to do specific business functions or processes of its business, reducing costs and getting expert professionals to do the work.
concepts.example: Rashtrapati Bhawan and Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi (Fig. 7.16) stand for two different moments in this history -- one built as the seat of British and now Indian government, the other a modern venue for national and international gatherings -- on a site that has been a centre of power since the Iron Age.

questions.a: Sample: Most of the chapter's cities are explained by one clear driver: Jamshedpur by iron ore, Bengaluru by its software firms and institutions, Agra by the Taj Mahal. Giving Delhi a layered history rather than one cause reflects that it is less a city with one origin story than a location that has been repeatedly chosen as a seat of power across very different eras, and each layer -- forts and roads, then railways and electricity, then ministries and research centres -- still shapes the city today.

concepts.name: Cities as cultural hubs
concepts.description: How cities create a shared, blended culture by drawing people from many regions, the chapter's examples of vada pav and Kolkata's Durga Puja, and the facilities -- cultural centres, libraries, museums, sports stadiums -- that cities build for cultural enrichment.
concepts.idea: A city's culture is rarely made in the city itself -- it is stitched together out of what the people who move there bring with them, which is why a snack from Mumbai's textile mills or a festival from British-era Kolkata can end up defining the whole city.
concepts.rule: Cities draw people from various regions, and they create a potpourri of culture, languages, customs, traditions, food and festivals, which begin to be shared along with shared spaces. Cities also allocate resources to create other types of facilities -- cultural centres, libraries, museums and sports stadiums -- which become hubs for the enrichment of socio-cultural aspects, and spaces are created for national and international gatherings for sharing knowledge and ideas, giving inhabitants new and exciting experiences that help them interact, build relationships and form networks.
concepts.example: Vada pav is a famous snack from Mumbai in which a Maharashtrian-style potato dumpling is placed inside a pav (where pao or bread and potatoes are Portuguese); this easy-to-make, easy-to-carry, easy-to-eat snack became very popular among workers in Mumbai's textile mills. Kolkata, once the capital of British-ruled India, still has institutions from that era such as the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial, and its annual Durga Puja, a five-day festival held every autumn, was inscribed on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2021.

questions.a: Sample: The two examples show the same blending of culture happening at very different scales. Vada pav is private and everyday -- something an individual eats without thinking about where its parts came from -- while Durga Puja is public and organised, a five-day festival recognised internationally by UNESCO. Using both together tells the reader that a city's cultural mixing is not confined to grand, visible occasions like festivals; it also lives in small, ordinary things like a snack sold on a street corner. A reader given only the festival example might think cultural hubs are about monuments and events; the food example corrects that by showing the same process at work in daily life.
s: Describes vada pav as a small, everyday, private example

questions.q: Analyse whether the cultural mixing shown through vada pav and Durga Puja happens through the same mechanism as the cultural facilities described through libraries, museums, cultural centres and sports stadiums, or through a different one.
questions.a: Sample: Vada pav and Durga Puja arose organically. Vada pav was assembled informally out of a Maharashtrian dumpling and a Portuguese-derived pav, and became popular among textile mill workers without any city authority designing or funding it; Durga Puja continued as a long-observed autumn tradition that only later received UNESCO recognition. Libraries, museums, cultural centres and sports stadiums work differently: the chapter says cities 'allocate resources to create' these facilities, which is a deliberate, funded decision. So the chapter is actually describing two different mechanisms for how a city becomes a cultural hub -- one bottom-up, where mixing happens on its own as people from different regions live and work together, and one top-down, where the city deliberately builds venues for cultural life. A complete cultural hub, on the chapter's own account, needs both: the organic mixing supplies the shared identity and traditions, while the built facilities supply the spaces that let that identity be experienced, gathered around and preserved.
s: Identifies vada pav and/or Durga Puja as arising organically, without deliberate planning or funding by a city authority
Identifies libraries, museums, cultural centres and stadiums as arising from cities deliberately allocating resources
States that these are two different mechanisms -- bottom-up mixing and top-down provision

Kolkata's identity as a cultural hub is built from its long history as the former capital of British-ruled India, with institutions like the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial, and from the festival itself having been observed every autumn for far longer than the recognition has existed. UNESCO's 2021 inscription records and honours a cultural practice the chapter presents as already established, rather than creating that practice. The recognition may well amplify Kolkata's cultural identity going forward, drawing more visitors and attention, but the chapter's own sequence -- the festival described first, its history and character explained, and the inscription mentioned last as a fact about it -- treats the inscription as an outcome, not an origin.

concepts.name: Challenges faced by cities
concepts.description: The pressures rapid population growth puts on a city's resources and infrastructure, air quality and crime, what slums are and why they form, government efforts such as the Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana, and Bengaluru's lake crisis and its community-led revival.
concepts.idea: Every advantage a city offers for concentrating people is also what concentrates its problems, so the same crowding that creates jobs and culture also creates strain on air, water, housing and safety.
concepts.rule: The influx of large populations into cities puts pressure on resources, and increased demand for food, water, energy and housing strains infrastructure; narrow and poorly maintained roads, unplanned residential areas with poor access to water, sanitation, energy and waste management, a growing number of vehicles, and rising temperatures from 'heat islands' are among the problems urban areas face, along with rising pollution, waste, and higher crime rates linked to population density and economic inequality. Slums are overcrowded city settlements with poor housing and limited water, sanitation and other municipal services, generally growing near a city's periphery, railway tracks or industrial areas where vacant land is available, due to a lack of enough affordable housing; slum dwellers often support cities through informal work such as vegetable vending, domestic help, laundry services, construction and plumbing. The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a numerical scale that reports air quality by combining data on pollutants such as PM2.5, PM10, carbon monoxide and sulfur dioxide into a single value; the higher the AQI, the greater the pollution and the health risk.
concepts.example: The National Capital Region frequently records AQI levels over 400, far above the safe limit of 50. Bengaluru once had around 1,000 lakes, but rapid urbanisation, overuse of groundwater, lack of rainwater harvesting and encroachment of lake beds reduced the number to about 200, with lakes such as Bellandur and Varthur getting covered in foam, releasing toxic gases and even catching fire; non-profit organisations, Resident Welfare Associations and communities have since worked to revive the lakes through desilting, repairing bunds with natural materials, clearing drainage channels, planting native plant species and restocking fish, and the government's Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana provides affordable housing to economically weaker households.

questions.q: The chapter describes Bengaluru's lake crisis as caused by 'poor urban planning' and its revival as led by 'non-profit organisations, Resident Welfare Associations and communities' rather than by the city government. questions.a: Sample: The chapter's account puts the cause at the level of planning decisions -- overuse of groundwater, lack of rainwater harvesting, encroachment of lake beds -- which are the kind of large-scale choices a city government or developers make, or fail to prevent. This is a striking gap -- the chapter does not credit any government body with reversing the damage it blames on planning failures. It suggests either that the chapter sees community action as genuinely the most effective response to this kind of damage, or that it is quietly acknowledging that governments have not adequately addressed a problem they had a hand in creating, leaving citizens to do the work instead. concepts.name: Planning cities: Jaipur, Singapore and India's urban redevelopment
concepts.description: What an urban planner must consider, the historical planning of Jaipur as the 'Pink City' and the dynamic planning of Singapore, and how present-day Indian projects such as the Sabarmati Riverfront and Gangtok's MG Road, along with new technologies, continue that work of planning cities for the future.
concepts.idea: A well-planned city is not one that got everything right once, but one built to keep adapting -- the same idea links a grid laid out in 1727 and a plan updated every five years four centuries later.
concepts.rule: Urban planners must address factors such as how many people live in a place, what jobs they have, what transportation they require, where homes, businesses, parks and public facilities should be located, and what public safety provisions are needed. Jaipur, the 'Pink City', was designed from 1727 by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, chief architect and urban planner appointed by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II, using a grid pattern of rectangular blocks called chowkris aligned to the cardinal directions, with wide streets, open spaces, gardens and nine public squares, enclosed by a 20-foot wall with seven gates, its major streets built in pink sandstone for a uniform, cohesive look. Singapore, with over 8,000 people per sq km, uses a Concept Plan looking up to 40 years ahead and a Master Plan updated every 5 years, promotes mixed-use spaces, mass public transport and sustainable high-rise buildings with rooftop and vertical gardens that earned it the title of a 'garden city', and integrates senior housing with healthcare, childcare and green spaces, making it one of the world's 'blue zone' cities.
concepts.example: In India, urban redevelopment projects such as Ahmedabad's Sabarmati Riverfront, with its promenades, parks, markets and the pedestrian-and-cycle Atal Bridge, and Gangtok's pedestrian-only Mahatma Gandhi Road, blend ecology, technology and public utility; the chapter's closing reflection adds that ICT tools such as intelligent traffic systems, digital surveillance, online grievance redressal and solar-powered public spaces are needed to make cities more sustainable as they balance growth with care for people and Nature.
